Theater of Operations of the North Sea was the scene of the battles carried out in the North Sea between the naval forces of the Royal Navy (English Navy) and the Kaiserliche Marine (German Navy) during the World War I.The culminating episode was the battle of Jutland; after that the German high seas fleet was confined to ports following the "fleet in being" strategy, until after signing the armistice it moved to Scapa Flow (in the Orkney Islands), where the Germans sank it in Scapa Flow to prevent it from falling into Allied hands.
The English naval blockade
The North Sea was the main theater of operations of the naval war of the First World War, where they faced the British Grand Fleet (Great Fleet) and the German Hochseeflotte (High Seas Fleet).
The Royal Navy, larger, tried to maintain the naval blockade of the German ports in order not to give their opponents the opportunity to go to sea and to cut off the trade routes. The Northern Patrol and the Dover Patrol blocked access to the North Sea and the English Channel respectively.
The German ships were safe in their bases, protected by mined reefs, and only occasionally attempted to engage the English fleet in the hope of weakening it or intercepting any enemy convoys. The British were content to maintain the blockade and, when possible, damage the German fleet to allow their ships to be used elsewhere.
The fights
A notable incident was the sinking of the English scout ship HMS Pathfinder, torpedoed by a German submarine and sinking with most of the crew; the ship had the unenviable distinction of being the first to be sunk by a torpedo fired from a submarine.
The main confrontations were the first and second battles of Heligoland, the battle of Banc Dogger, and that of Jutland. In general, the British, although they did not achieve tactical successes, were able to maintain the blockade and to keep the German navy in their ports. For this, however, it was necessary to involve the vast majority of the large units of the Royal Navy, since the danger of the Hochseeflotte remained constant throughout the war. There were also attempts to block some harbors permanently, sinking some large ships in the approaches, but they were unsuccessful and costly in terms of loss of human life.
Even the patrol operations carried out in the North Sea had their risks, especially due to the German submarines; in the action on 22 September 1914 a single submarine sank three British battlecruisers of the Cressy class (HMS Cressy, HMS Abukir and HMS Hogue), killing 60 officers and 1,400 crew members.. Another threat to the ships were sea mines, one of which sank the battleship HMS Audacious during a training exercise, and its loss, with no casualties among the crew, was long kept secret.
The bombardment of Yarmouth, of November 3, 1914, was an attack by the Hochseeflotte against the port facilities of the English city of Great Yarmouth. The town suffered little damage as German shells fell on the beach and the action was halted by British destroyers. A British submarine left port to attack the German ships, but struck a mine laid by the German minesweeper SMS Stralsund and sank. Later, a German cruiser struck two mines while entering her harbor and sank.
This action was followed by the Scarborough, Hartlepool and Whitby Bombardment of 16 December 1914, a naval bombardment carried out by the Hochseeflotte against the port towns of Scarborough, Hartlepool and Whitby, which caused 137 deaths and 592 wounded, many of them civilians. The Scouting force immediately went in pursuit of the German fleet, but was unable to attack it due to a shortage of battlecruisers and communication problems. Both the Germans and the British were unhappy that they had not effectively defeated the enemy. Admiral Friedrich von Ingenohl's reputation suffered from the apparent display of timidity in action. The captain of the SMS Moltke expressed his disappointment and stated that "Ingenohl had withdrawn because he was afraid of the eleven British destroyers that could be knocked out ... under the present management we will not get any results". The official German history criticizes Ingenohl for not having used his reconnaissance forces to determine the forces deployed by the British; he had taken a decision which, not only could have endangered his forces on the English coast, but also lost the opportunity to achieve an important secure victory. The attack had a lot of resonance in Britain and created a wave of indignation against Germany.
At the Battle of Dogger Bank on 24 January 1915, a German force returning from bombardment of the British coast (consisting of the battlecruisers SMS Seydlitz, SMS Moltke and SMS Derfflinger, the battlecruiser SMS Blucher and light cruisers) was intercepted by a flotilla of British battlecruisers, after being closely followed by a force of Royal Navy cruisers and destroyers patrolling the area (the Harwich Force, consisting of the battle cruisers HMS Lion, HMS Tiger, HMS Princess Royal, HMS New Zealand and HMS Indomitable). The SMS Blucher, was seriously damaged and then sank, while a decoding error of the signals issued by the English admiral David Beatty allowed the German ships to reach their port.
The bombing of Yarmouth and Lowestoft, of April 24, 1916, was an attack by the Hochseeflotte against the port facilities of the English cities of Yarmouth and Lowestoft. The objective of the attack was to attract the British fleet to destroy it in combat. In support, a German Zeppelin attacked Norwich, Lincoln, Harwich and Ipswich. The attack was coordinated with the Irish Easter Rising, after the agreements between Irish and German nationalists. The objective was not achieved and the action was settled with limited damage on both sides

The Zeebrugge raid was one of several measures taken by the Royal Navy during the First World War to block the access channel to the port of Bruges, which was widely used by the Kaiserliche Marine as a base for submarines and light ships, by sinking a ship loaded with cement at the entrance. This raid was followed by the first Oostende raid (Operation ZO) which was an action carried out by the Royal Navy in order to block access to the port of Oostende. The proximity of these ports to the British supply routes through the English Channel was a constant threat to the continuity of the war effort of the British Expeditionary Force (British Expeditionary Force). The attacks were launched at the end of the spring of 1918. The first attempt to block Ostend and Zeebrugge simultaneously was made on 23 April, but both operations failed. Three weeks later a second attack (Operation VS) was carried out, which was more successful with the sinking of a ship in the harbor access channel, but without being able to completely cut the passage to Bruges. These attacks were preceded by the landing of teams of Royal Marines, tasked with neutralizing the port's defences, but it came at a high cost in terms of human lives to achieve little result, so that the two ports were never really blocked (Zeebrugge was only for a few hours, Ostend for a few days after the first attack, and in the second attack, until German engineers dredged a canal parallel to the first). New plans were made to attack the area during the summer of 1918, but were not implemented and German bases in the area remained a constant threat until the end of the conflict, when the city was liberated by French and British ground forces.
Consequences
leads the march of Hochseeflotte cruisers to Scapa Flow on 21 November 1918, following the surrender of Germany.]]
The sinking of the German fleet in Scapa Flow took place at the base of the Royal Navy in Scapa Flow (Scotland) after the end of the First World War. According to the terms of the armistice, the Hochseeflotte was to be confined to the area until the fate of the ships was decided. Faced with the fear that the units would be divided between the navies of the victorious powers, Admiral Ludwig von Reuter decided to sink the fleet.
On June 21, 1919, the crew of the German ships began to sink their ships; the British ships at the base managed to run some ships aground in shallow water, but were unable to prevent the sinking of 52 units out of 74. The last ship sunk, the battlecruiser SMS Hindenburg, sank at 5:00 p.m. Nine German sailors died and about 16 were injured in their ships for not obeying the order to stop the sinking given by patrol boats of the Royal Navy.
During the afternoon 1,774 German sailors were rounded up and transported aboard warships at Invergordon. A directive was issued stating that the Germans would be treated as prisoners of war for breaking the truce, and they were sent to the Nigg prison camp.
